journal_name: ACM Transactions on Asian and Low-Resource Language Information Processing

abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel theoretical framework for addressing the fundamental challenges in low-resource language processing, an area that has long been hampered by data scarcity and linguistic diversity. Existing approaches predominantly rely on transfer learning paradigms derived from high-resource language settings, which fail to account for the structural and typological differences inherent in under-resourced languages. We propose the Linguistic Typology-Aware Transfer (LTAT) framework, which establishes a formal connection between language typological features and optimal transfer strategies through information-theoretic analysis. Our theoretical investigation reveals that conventional cross-lingual alignment methods implicitly assume typological uniformity, leading to suboptimal performance when applied to typologically distant language pairs. We formalize the relationship between linguistic distance metrics and transfer learning efficacy, proving that adaptive transfer mechanisms based on typological clustering significantly outperform uniform transfer approaches. The framework introduces the concept of transfer difficulty coefficients derived from morphological complexity and syntactic divergence measures. Experimental validation on a typologically diverse set of 15 low-resource Asian languages demonstrates that our theoretical predictions align closely with empirical observations, achieving an average improvement of 23% in machine translation quality and 31% in cross-lingual retrieval tasks. This work establishes a principled foundation for designing language-specific transfer strategies and opens new research directions in computational linguistics for endangered language preservation.

Subword-level representations have become the dominant approach in neural machine translation for low-resource languages, yet existing theoretical analyses fail to adequately explain the observed variance in performance across different language families. This paper provides a rigorous theoretical analysis of why subword tokenization strategies exhibit inconsistent behavior when applied to morphologically rich Asian languages. We extend the established information-theoretic framework for vocabulary selection by introducing a novel measure termed Morphological Entropy Robustness (MER), which quantifies the sensitivity of tokenization quality to corpus size variations. Our analysis demonstrates that byte-pair encoding (BPE) and its variants suffer from a fundamental limitation: they optimize for compression efficiency rather than morphological integrity, leading to fragmented representations in agglutinative languages. We prove theoretically that vocabulary sizes optimized through our MER criterion achieve superior generalization by maintaining morphological unit coherence. Based on this theoretical foundation, we propose the Adaptive Morphological Subword (AMS) tokenization method, which dynamically adjusts vocabulary composition based on estimated morphological complexity. Experiments on Thai, Vietnamese, and Myanmar language translation tasks validate our theoretical predictions, showing that AMS achieves consistent improvements of 8-15% in BLEU scores while reducing vocabulary fragmentation by 40%. This analysis provides actionable insights for language resource development in low-resource scenarios.

We present LLM4LRL, a comprehensive multimodal system architecture designed specifically for low-resource language processing tasks that integrates large language model capabilities with culturally-aware knowledge retrieval. Existing NLP systems for Asian low-resource languages typically adopt a modular pipeline approach, treating language modeling, speech processing, and information retrieval as isolated components. This fragmentation leads to significant error propagation and fails to capture the rich multimodal context inherent in many low-resource language use cases. Our proposed architecture introduces a unified encoder-decoder framework with language-specific adapters that maintain cross-lingual alignment while preserving language-specific features. The system incorporates a novel Cultural Knowledge Graph module that augments language understanding with culturally contextualized information, addressing a critical gap in current approaches to Asian language processing. Speech processing capabilities are integrated through a cross-modal attention mechanism that enables seamless text-speech interaction for under-resourced languages. The architecture supports dynamic vocabulary expansion, allowing continuous integration of new linguistic variants and dialects without full model retraining. Comprehensive evaluation on benchmark datasets covering Indonesian, Malay, Tagalog, and Khmer demonstrates that LLM4RL achieves state-of-the-art performance in language modeling (perplexity reduction of 18%), machine translation (平均+12 BLEU), and cross-lingual information retrieval (recall@10 improvement of 27%). The system has been deployed for language preservation initiatives in three Southeast Asian communities.

This paper introduces an enhanced neural machine translation system specifically optimized for low-resource Asian languages, addressing the persistent challenge of inadequate parallel corpora through innovative data augmentation and model architecture modifications. Current state-of-the-art systems for low-resource translation rely heavily on back-translation and self-training, which suffer from error accumulation when applied to languages with limited initial data quality. We propose the Adaptive Back-Translation with Validation (ABTV) system, featuring three key innovations: (1) a confidence-weighted sentence selection mechanism that filters noisy synthetic data using perplexity-based quality estimation, (2) a cross-lingual adapter module that facilitates efficient knowledge transfer from related high-resource languages, and (3) an ensemble decoding strategy that combines multiple translation hypotheses based on uncertainty estimation. The system incorporates specialized handling for tonal languages (Vietnamese, Thai) through tone-aware positional encodings and for script多样化 languages through Unicode normalization with dialect-specific adaptation layers. Extensive experiments on WAT2023 and ALTA 2023 benchmarks demonstrate that ABTV consistently outperforms existing methods across eight Asian language pairs, with improvements ranging from 6.4 to 18.7 BLEU points over strong baselines. The system achieves particularly significant gains for extremely low-resource languages (with less than 50K parallel sentences), demonstrating robust generalization through effective utilization of linguistic relatedness among language families.
